Look at the individuals of one variety or sub-variety of any of our older cultivated plants and animals. One of the first things that strikes us is that they generally differ far more from one another than the individuals of any one species or variety do in nature.

Consider how many plants and animals have been cultivated, and how they have varied through all ages under the most different climates and treatment. I think we are driven to conclude that this greater variability comes from raising our domestic productions under conditions of life that are less uniform than, and somewhat different from, the conditions their parent-species met in nature. There is also, I think, some probability in the view put forward by Andrew Knight that the variability may be partly connected with an excess of food.

It seems pretty clear that organic beings must be exposed to the new conditions of life for several generations before they show any appreciable amount of variation, and that once an organisation has begun to vary, it generally continues to vary for many generations. No case is on record of a variable being ceasing to be variable under cultivation. Our oldest cultivated plants, such as wheat, still often yield new varieties, and our oldest domesticated animals are still capable of rapid improvement or modification.

I was born in Tuckahoe, near Hillsborough, and about twelve miles from Easton, in Talbot county, Maryland. I have no accurate knowledge of my age, because I have never seen an authentic record containing it. By far the larger part of the slaves know as little of their ages as horses know of theirs, and it is the wish of most masters within my knowledge to keep their slaves ignorant of it. I do not remember ever meeting a slave who could tell his birthday. The nearest they come is planting-time, harvest-time, cherry-time, spring-time, or fall-time.

Not knowing my own age was a source of unhappiness to me even in childhood. The white children could tell their ages. I could not tell why I should be deprived of the same privilege, and I was not allowed to ask my master about it. He deemed all such inquiries on the part of a slave improper and impertinent, and evidence of a restless spirit.

The nearest estimate I can give makes me now between twenty-seven and twenty-eight years of age. I come to this from hearing my master say, some time during 1835, that I was about seventeen years old.

I think you may like to know something of my father's person and character. He had an excellent constitution of body, was of middle stature but well set and very strong. He was ingenious, could draw prettily, was skilled a little in music, and had a clear, pleasing voice, so that when he played psalm tunes on his violin and sang along, as he sometimes did in an evening after the business of the day was over, it was extremely agreeable to hear. To get a clear and just idea of the design and end of government, suppose a small number of persons settled in some sequestered part of the earth, unconnected with the rest. They will then represent the first peopling of any country, or of the world. In this state of natural liberty, society will be their first thought. A thousand motives will push them toward it. The strength of one man is so unequal to his wants, and his mind so unfitted for perpetual solitude, that he is soon obliged to seek the assistance and relief of another, who in his turn requires the same.

Four or five united could raise a tolerable dwelling in the midst of a wilderness. One man alone might labour out the common period of life without accomplishing anything. When he had felled his timber he could not remove it, nor erect it once it was removed; hunger in the meantime would drive him from his work, and every different want would call him a different way. Disease, or even ordinary misfortune, would be death: though neither might be mortal in itself, either would disable him from living, and reduce him to a state in which he might rather be said to perish than to die.

I think we may safely trust a good deal more than we do. We may give up just as much care of ourselves as we honestly give elsewhere. Nature is as well adapted to our weakness as to our strength. The incessant anxiety and strain some people live under is an almost incurable form of disease.

We are made to exaggerate the importance of the work we do; and yet how much is not done by us! Or, what if we had been taken sick? How vigilant we are! Determined not to live by faith if we can avoid it, on the alert all day long, at night we unwillingly say our prayers and commit ourselves to uncertainties. So thoroughly and sincerely are we compelled to live, reverencing our life and denying the possibility of change. This is the only way, we say; but there are as many ways as there are radii that can be drawn from one centre. All change is a miracle to contemplate, but it is a miracle taking place every instant.

Confucius said, "To know that we know what we know, and that we do not know what we do not know, that is true knowledge." When one man has reduced a fact of the imagination to a fact of his understanding, I foresee that all men at length establish their lives on that basis.

By the time I had mastered the language of this water, and had come to know every trifling feature along the great river as familiarly as I knew the letters of the alphabet, I had made a valuable acquisition. But I had lost something too, something that could never be restored to me while I lived. All the grace, the beauty, the poetry had gone out of the majestic river!

I still keep in mind a certain wonderful sunset I witnessed when steamboating was new to me. A broad expanse of the river was turned to blood. In the middle distance the red hue brightened into gold, and through it a solitary log came floating, black and conspicuous. In one place a long, slanting mark lay sparkling on the water; in another the surface was broken by boiling, tumbling rings as many-tinted as an opal. Where the ruddy flush was faintest lay a smooth spot covered with graceful circles and radiating lines, ever so delicately traced. The shore on our left was densely wooded, and the somber shadow that fell from the forest was broken in one place by a long, ruffled trail that shone like silver. High above the forest wall a clean-stemmed dead tree waved a single leafy bough that glowed like a flame in the unobstructed splendor flowing from the sun. There were graceful curves, reflected images, woody heights, soft distances; and over the whole scene, far and near, the dissolving lights drifted steadily, enriching it every passing moment with new marvels of coloring.
